items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Union County, AR
items.meta: Union County, AR mineral owner? El Dorado's 1921 Smackover boom left thousands of small legacy interests, now overlapping a lithium brine build-out. Get a written offer.

sections.html:
El Dorado has been an oil town since 1921, and the same Smackover Formation that made it one is now the center of a lithium brine build-out that touches almost every old royalty deed in the county.

Union County is where the Arkansas oil business started. The 1921 discovery at El Dorado turned a farm town into a boomtown almost overnight, and companies that are still household names in the industry, Murphy Oil among them, trace their roots to that field. A century later the Smackover Formation under the county is doing something different: instead of oil, operators are pulling lithium-rich brine out of the same limestone and pumping it toward processing plants built to feed the battery supply chain.

For a mineral owner, that history shows up as layers. Some tracts still carry small legacy oil and gas interests from the 1920s through 1980s, often split many ways across heirs who never formally probated the estate. Other tracts sit inside newer brine unit boundaries staked by Standard Lithium, ExxonMobil, and other operators working the South Arkansas play. A few carry both. Knowing which kind of interest you hold, and what it is actually producing or leased for, is the first step before any conversation about selling.

sections.title: Legacy Smackover Oil vs. Brine Minerals
sections.html:
Arkansas law and most modern lease forms treat oil and gas rights and the brine or 'other minerals' rights as separate bundles, even when the same instrument once conveyed both. A deed from the 1930s oil boom may say nothing specific about lithium, bromine, or brine, which means ownership of those rights can hinge on the exact conveyance language and how courts and title examiners have read similar Smackover deeds. Bromine production has operated in this corner of Arkansas for decades, so there is precedent for how 'other minerals' clauses get interpreted, but every deed still needs its own read.

This is the reason offers on Union County tracts vary so much even between neighbors. A parcel with clean brine rights inside an active unit is a different asset than a parcel where the mineral deed is ambiguous or where a working interest was carved out generations ago and never released.

sections.title: What's Actually Moving in the County
sections.html: El Dorado remains a working oil field with strippers and secondary-recovery wells still on the books, and royalty statements from those legacy units tend to be small and declining, which is normal for a field this old. The newer activity is brine-focused: permitting, unit formation, and infrastructure tied to lithium extraction have picked up meaningfully in the South Arkansas Smackover trend that runs through Union, Columbia, and neighboring counties. Depending on where a tract sits relative to unit boundaries and processing infrastructure, that can materially change how a buyer prices the interest, but any number quoted to you should be tied to comparable recent activity and hedged to reflect that the play is still developing, not a fixed promise.

sections.title: Getting Your Union County Interest in Order
sections.html:
Start at the Union County Circuit Clerk's office in El Dorado, where the deed and probate records live. Many mineral tracts here were never formally divided among heirs after the original owner passed, which means several family members may hold undivided fractional interests without a clean paper trail. If your interest passed through inheritance, a title check will usually surface whether an affidavit of heirship or probate is needed before a sale can close.

Once ownership is clear, a serious buyer will want a copy of your most recent division order or royalty statement if you have one, the legal description (section, township, range), and any lease or brine unit paperwork you've received. If you've never received anything, that's useful information too. It tells a buyer your interest may be unleased, which changes how it's valued relative to a producing tract.

faqs.q: You own oil rights from a 1940s deed. Do you also own the lithium brine under your land?
faqs.a: It depends on the exact language in your deed and any later conveyances. Some older Union County mineral deeds are broad enough to cover brine and other dissolved minerals; others were written narrowly around oil and gas and leave brine rights ambiguous or with a different owner. A title review of your specific instrument is the only way to answer this with confidence.

faqs.q: Why is your royalty check from the old El Dorado field so small?
faqs.a: Legacy Smackover oil wells in Union County are a century into production and decline the way any mature field does. Small, declining checks from a stripper-well unit are typical and don't necessarily reflect the value of the underlying mineral interest, especially if newer brine activity has picked up nearby.

faqs.q: How do you know if your land is inside a brine unit?
faqs.a: Unit orders are filed with the Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission and recorded at the county clerk. If you've received a lease offer, division order, or unitization notice referencing brine or 'other minerals,' that's a strong signal. If you're unsure, the acquisition desk can help you check the unit boundaries against your legal description before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Your mineral interest is split between several cousins. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes, undivided fractional interests are common in this county and can be purchased individually or together. Each heir typically needs to be identified with clear title, which sometimes requires an affidavit of heirship if the estate was never probated.

faqs.q: Is a lithium brine offer valued differently than an oil and gas offer?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Brine value is tied to processing capacity, unit position, and the pace of the extraction build-out rather than a conventional well's decline curve, so comparisons should be made against recent brine-specific activity, not old oil comps.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Columbia County, AR
items.meta: Own oil, gas, or brine rights in Columbia County, Arkansas near Magnolia? The acquisition desk evaluates legacy Smackover production and lithium brine-adjacent tracts, and make a cash offer.

sections.html:
Columbia County, led by Magnolia, sits at the center of one of the most closely watched lithium brine developments in the country, layered on top of nearly a century of Smackover oil history.

Albemarle has operated a bromine extraction facility near Magnolia for decades, pulling the same Smackover Formation brine that's now drawing serious lithium development through the South West Arkansas project, a joint effort backed by Standard Lithium and Equinor spanning acreage across Columbia, Lafayette, and Nevada counties. That project has put Columbia County on the map in a way it hasn't been since the original oil boom, and it's changed the questions mineral owners here are asking.

But not every acre in the county is inside the active leasehold, and not every deed's mineral language actually covers brine the way it covers oil and gas. The acquisition desk underwrites Columbia County interests with both of those questions in mind before quoting anything.

sections.title: Legacy Smackover oil and gas production
sections.html:
Conventional oil and gas production in Columbia County follows the same broad pattern as the rest of the south Arkansas Smackover trend: wells drilled decades ago, now producing at stripper rates, with royalty interests that are frequently small and split among several heirs. This baseline value exists independent of any lithium activity, and it's where the acquisition desk starts every evaluation, checking current volumes and operator status against the well's full production history rather than what it may have paid when it was first drilled.

Fractional ownership is the norm rather than the exception here. Many Columbia County interests have passed through three or four generations without a formal partition, which means confirming exactly what percentage a given owner holds is often the first real step in any sale.

sections.title: Brine rights versus oil and gas rights: the deed language question
sections.html:
The single most important issue for a Columbia County mineral owner evaluating potential lithium value isn't whether the county has active brine development, it clearly does, it's whether the specific deed governing their tract actually extends to brine. Older instruments in this area were drafted with conventional oil, gas, and sometimes casinghead gas in mind, decades before brine-hosted lithium was commercially relevant anywhere. Some of that language is broad enough that a title attorney would read it to include brine as an "other mineral"; other deeds are narrow enough that it clearly wouldn't.

This isn't a formality. A tract sitting inside the South West Arkansas leasehold with brine-inclusive deed language is a meaningfully different asset than the same physical tract with narrower language, even though both owners might describe their property the same way. The acquisition desk reviews this distinction directly as part of any offer involving potential brine relevance, and the acquisition desk does not price in speculative lithium upside on a deed that doesn't clearly support it.

sections.title: What proximity to Magnolia does and doesn't tell you
sections.html:
Being located near Magnolia puts an owner in the right general region for the South West Arkansas project, but it doesn't automatically mean a specific parcel sits inside the active leasehold currently being developed by Standard Lithium and Equinor. Leasehold blocks have defined boundaries, and formation depth and brine chemistry vary enough across the county that general proximity is a starting point for the conversation, not the answer to it.

The acquisition desk checks actual current leasehold and permit maps against an owner's legal description before making any claim about brine relevance. If a tract turns out to sit outside the active footprint, the acquisition desk says so rather than pricing in upside the geology and the leasehold map don't support.

sections.title: Columbia County Circuit Clerk records and courthouse research
sections.html:
Magnolia serves as both the site of the county's major bromine and emerging lithium infrastructure and the county seat where deed, lease, probate, and division order records are filed. Given how much Columbia County mineral ownership has fractionalized across generations, the acquisition desk leans heavily on these records to confirm a specific owner's exact share before making an offer, working from a deed, a division order, an old lease, or a probate reference, whatever exists.

The acquisition desk also verifies whether any given tract's oil and gas lease is separate from, or silent on, brine rights specifically, since that distinction often isn't clear from a division order alone and requires pulling the underlying deed.

faqs.q: Does your mineral deed in Columbia County cover brine and lithium, or just oil and gas?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the specific language in your deed. Older instruments vary significantly on this point, and the acquisition desk reviews your deed's actual language as part of evaluating your interest rather than assuming either way.

faqs.q: Is your land inside the South West Arkansas lithium project's active leasehold?
faqs.a: It may or may not be, depending on your exact section relative to current leasehold boundaries. The acquisition desk checks current maps against your legal description before making any claim about relevance.

faqs.q: Your family has an old oil royalty near Magnolia. Is that connected to the lithium brine activity?
faqs.a: Generally they're separate, though related, revenue streams from the same underlying Smackover formation. The acquisition desk evaluates your legacy oil and gas interest and any potential brine relevance independently, as part of the same offer.

faqs.q: How fractionalized are typical Columbia County mineral interests?
faqs.a: Very commonly split across three or more generations of heirs without formal partition. The acquisition desk is set up to confirm exact fractional shares through Circuit Clerk records and can purchase individual shares without requiring the whole family to act together.

faqs.q: What happens if your tract turns out to have no realistic brine or lithium relevance?
faqs.a: The acquisition desk will tell you directly. Your legacy oil and gas interest, if any, is still evaluated and priced on its own merits, the acquisition desk just won't price in speculative brine upside the leasehold map and geology don't support.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Ouachita County, AR
items.meta: Ouachita County, AR mineral rights near Camden and the Smackover trend. Old oil-era deeds, bromine history, and new brine leasing. Get a written offer today.

sections.html:
Camden sits on the edge of the same Smackover trend that runs through El Dorado, and the county's mineral records still carry the fingerprints of an oil boom that peaked before most current owners were born.

Ouachita County's mineral history runs through Camden, the county seat, and a scatter of smaller Smackover-era fields that produced steadily for decades before settling into stripper-well status. It's a quieter corner of the play than Union County next door, but the same formation and the same emerging lithium-brine interest extend across the county line, which means landowners here are increasingly getting offer letters and lease requests they don't recognize the source of.

Ownership in Ouachita County tends to be fractional and inherited. A single 40-acre or 80-acre tract from an original homestead may now be held by a dozen descendants scattered across several states, most of whom have never seen a division order and don't know whether their interest is leased, held by production, or sitting dormant.

sections.title: A Field That Never Fully Shut Down
sections.html:
Camden-area production dates back to the same wave of Smackover discoveries that built El Dorado, though on a smaller scale. Many of the wells still on the books here are late-life producers held together by low lifting costs rather than new drilling, and royalty checks from them are typically modest and declining. That's the baseline most Ouachita County mineral owners are used to, and it's part of why interest from the newer lithium-brine side of the business tends to catch people off guard.

The brine trend that's driving activity in Union and Columbia counties reaches into parts of Ouachita County as well, and operators evaluating the South Arkansas Smackover play have been acquiring leasehold and mineral positions across county lines rather than treating each county as its own market.

sections.title: Reading Your Deed Before You Sign Anything
sections.html:
The single most common issue the acquisition desk sees on Ouachita County tracts is a deed that was written for oil and gas decades ago and never addresses brine, lithium, or 'other minerals' directly. Whether that older language covers the new activity is a legal question, not a formatting one, and it's worth getting a straight answer before signing a new lease or accepting an offer that assumes one interpretation over another.

It's also worth checking whether your interest is already under an old lease. Many Smackover-era leases from Ouachita County were written with broad habendum clauses that keep the lease alive as long as any well on the unit produces, even a marginal one. That can affect both what you're currently owed and what a buyer will pay for the underlying mineral interest.

sections.title: Clerk Records and Fractional Ownership
sections.html:
The Ouachita County Circuit Clerk in Camden holds the deed and probate records that establish who actually owns what. Because so much of the county's mineral estate passed through inheritance without formal probate, it's common for title work to turn up more heirs than a family expected, or to find that a great-aunt's share was never accounted for. None of that is unusual, and it doesn't stop a sale, but it does need to be resolved with clear documentation before a buyer can close.

If you have a royalty statement, a lease, or even an old letter referencing a well name or unit, hold onto it. Those details, along with your legal description, are what let a buyer evaluate your interest quickly instead of guessing.

faqs.q: How is Ouachita County connected to the Exxon and Standard Lithium projects you has read about?
faqs.a: Those projects are centered in neighboring Union and Columbia counties, but the Smackover brine trend they're built on extends into parts of Ouachita County. Whether your specific tract is affected depends on its position relative to current unit boundaries, which can shift as the play develops.

faqs.q: Your family's mineral rights were never split up after your grandfather passed. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It's common in this county and it's fixable. Most title issues of this kind are resolved with an affidavit of heirship or, in more complicated estates, a probate filing. The acquisition desk can walk you through what's needed for your specific situation.

faqs.q: Do you still own your minerals if your land was sold years ago?
faqs.a: Possibly. Mineral rights are frequently severed from surface ownership in this part of Arkansas, meaning a family can sell the farm while keeping the minerals underneath it. A title search of the Ouachita County records will confirm whether that happened on your tract.

faqs.q: What does a typical royalty check look like from an old Ouachita County well?
faqs.a: It varies with the well's age and current output, but most legacy Smackover wells in this county are late in their decline curve, so checks are usually modest. That's separate from what a buyer might pay for the interest itself, which also reflects nearby brine activity and lease status.

faqs.q: Should you sell your mineral rights or keep leasing them?
faqs.a: That depends on your goals. Leasing keeps you eligible for future royalty income but leaves you exposed to decline, unit changes, and the administrative burden of tracking a small interest across multiple owners. Selling converts an uncertain, long-tail income stream into a lump sum now. Neither is universally right, and the answer often comes down to how many years you expect to hold the interest and how comfortable you are with the volatility of legacy oil income.

faqs.q: Does a buyer need to see the physical well or just the paperwork?
faqs.a: Paperwork is what matters for valuation, not a site visit. A buyer works from your legal description, deed history, and any lease or royalty documentation, cross-referenced against Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission unit and permit records for that section, township, and range.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Lafayette County, AR
items.meta: Lafayette County, AR mineral owner near Lewisville or Stamps? Smackover-era oil deeds now sit in the middle of the South Arkansas lithium build-out. Get an offer.

sections.html:
Lewisville and Stamps sit near the Louisiana line in the thick of the South Arkansas Smackover trend, where old cotton-country mineral deeds are suddenly relevant to a lithium supply chain nobody was thinking about when they were written.

Lafayette County is smaller and quieter than its Union County neighbor, but it sits squarely inside the Smackover Formation's footprint, and its mineral history follows the same arc: oil leasing in the mid-20th century, decades of modest production, and now renewed attention tied to brine-based lithium extraction. Stamps, best known as Maya Angelou's childhood hometown, and the county seat of Lewisville both anchor communities where family farms were commonly leased for oil decades ago and where mineral rights have since scattered across generations of heirs.

Because the county borders Louisiana and sits at the edge of several operator acreage positions, mineral owners here sometimes get offers or lease requests that reference activity happening just across the line. Understanding whether your specific tract is inside an active unit, or simply near one, makes a real difference in how it should be valued.

sections.title: Cotton Land, Then Oil Leases, Then Silence
sections.html:
Much of Lafayette County's mineral ownership traces back to farmland that was leased for oil exploration decades ago, often with the surface still farmed while the mineral rights were leased or sold off separately. Many of those leases eventually went dormant as wells were plugged or production dropped below economic thresholds, leaving mineral owners with rights that haven't produced a royalty check in years but were never formally released either.

That kind of dormant interest is exactly the sort of tract that can look worthless on paper and still carry real value to a buyer, particularly if it sits inside or near a newer brine unit where the underlying formation, not the old well, is what matters now.

sections.title: The Louisiana Line and Unit Boundaries
sections.html:
Because Lafayette County borders Louisiana, some mineral tracts here sit near acreage positions and brine units that cross the state line or are administered alongside Louisiana operations. That can complicate title work slightly, since records and unit filings may need to be checked in more than one jurisdiction, but it doesn't change the fundamentals of how the county's Smackover-era deeds are read.

The practical takeaway is the same as elsewhere in the play: a tract's value depends heavily on its position relative to current and expected unit boundaries, and any figure quoted to you should be described as an estimate tied to comparable recent deals, not a fixed price.

sections.title: Title Work at the County Clerk in Lewisville
sections.html:
The Lafayette County Circuit Clerk's office in Lewisville holds the deed books, probate files, and lease recordings that establish ownership. As in most of south Arkansas, undivided fractional interests passed through inheritance are the norm rather than the exception, and it's common for a title search to turn up heirs who didn't know they held an interest at all.

If you're starting from a stack of old paperwork, or nothing at all, the useful first documents are a legal description (section, township, range), any old lease or division order you can find, and the names of any family members who might share the interest with you. From there, a buyer can tell you fairly quickly what kind of interest you're sitting on.

faqs.q: Your family's old lease near Stamps hasn't paid a royalty in over a decade. Is it still worth anything?
faqs.a: Possibly, and sometimes more than owners expect. A dormant lease from a plugged well doesn't necessarily mean the underlying mineral rights have no value, especially if the tract is near current brine or oil activity. The right way to find out is a review of your legal description against nearby unit and permit activity, not the old royalty history alone.

faqs.q: Does the Louisiana state line affect how your Lafayette County minerals are valued?
faqs.a: It can matter for title and unit-boundary purposes if your tract sits close to the line, since some operator activity is administered across both states. It doesn't change the underlying Arkansas mineral law that governs your deed.

faqs.q: You don't have any paperwork on your mineral rights, just family stories. Can you still help?
faqs.a: Yes. The acquisition desk can search the Lafayette County Circuit Clerk's deed and probate records using your family name and a general property location to reconstruct the legal description and ownership chain.

faqs.q: How many heirs typically share a mineral interest in this county?
faqs.a: It varies widely, but two to ten co-owners on a single tract is common where the original owner's estate was never formally probated. Each heir's share can usually be identified and purchased individually if the family prefers to sell separately.

faqs.q: Is there active drilling in Lafayette County right now, or is it mostly legacy production?
faqs.a: Most conventional oil and gas activity in the county is legacy production from decades-old units, with modest and declining royalty checks. The activity to watch is on the brine side, where operator interest in the South Arkansas Smackover trend has been picking up unit formation and leasing near the Union and Columbia county lines.

faqs.q: What paperwork speeds up a sale of your mineral interest?
faqs.a: A legal description, your most recent division order or royalty statement if available, any lease document referencing your tract, and proof of how the interest passed to you, whether that's a deed, a will, or an affidavit of heirship. Missing pieces aren't a dealbreaker; a buyer can usually help track them down through the county clerk.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Faulkner County, AR
items.meta: Own oil, gas, or mineral rights in Faulkner County, Arkansas? The acquisition desk evaluates core Fayetteville Shale legacy interests countywide and make a straightforward cash offer.

sections.html:
Faulkner County, led by Conway, sits at the structural core of the Fayetteville Shale play, one of the most heavily drilled counties in the entire trend.

Between roughly 2005 and 2012, Southwestern Energy and a handful of other operators drilled through Faulkner County about as densely as anywhere in the Fayetteville Shale, and the results generally matched the effort: this was, and remains, one of the strongest-performing counties in the play. That history means Faulkner County mineral owners are more likely than owners almost anywhere else in the state to hold an interest tied to a well with real, substantial production behind it, even though most of those wells are now more than a decade past their peak.

The county has also grown fast. Conway, home to the University of Central Arkansas and Hendrix College, has expanded steadily, and towns like Greenbrier have grown right alongside it. That growth has put mineral ownership questions in front of families who might otherwise never have thought about what's under land that's since been developed, sold, or subdivided.

sections.title: The most heavily drilled part of the Fayetteville Shale
sections.html:
Faulkner County sits inside the thickest, most productive part of the Fayetteville Shale, and well density here during the boom years was among the highest anywhere in the play. Communities throughout the county, from Conway itself out to Enola, Greenbrier, and Guy, saw substantial leasing and drilling activity, and a large share of that leasehold was actually developed rather than left dormant, unlike some of the play's fringe counties.

That doesn't mean every Faulkner County interest is currently generating strong income. Fayetteville Shale wells decline steeply after their first few years, and even the county's best original wells are now producing at a small fraction of their initial rate. The acquisition desk prices interests off current, decline-adjusted production, not the well's historical peak during the boom.

sections.title: Urban growth, mineral severance, and confirming what you actually own
sections.html:
As Conway and Greenbrier have grown, some land that once held straightforward rural mineral interests has been subdivided for housing or sold multiple times for commercial development. The mineral estate doesn't automatically transfer the same way the surface does in those transactions, meaning some owners assume they still hold minerals under land their family sold years ago when they actually don't, and others assume they lost mineral rights that were in fact reserved and still belong to them.

The acquisition desk checks the specific deed chain for a Faulkner County tract as a standard part of any evaluation, since confirming the interest is actually there, and actually belongs to the person the acquisition desk is talking to, has to come before any conversation about price.

sections.title: Operator history: Southwestern Energy, Flywheel Energy, and BKV Corporation
sections.html:
Southwestern Energy, through its SEECO subsidiary, drilled most of the original Fayetteville Shale wells across Faulkner County. Southwestern sold that entire Fayetteville Shale position to Flywheel Energy, backed by Kayne Anderson, in 2018, and BKV Corporation acquired Flywheel's Fayetteville Shale assets in 2021. If your family's royalty statements have shown more than one operator name over the years, this sequence of transactions is almost certainly why.

The acquisition desk verifies current operator and production status directly with the state rather than relying on whatever name last appeared on a statement, since it's common for owners to have outdated information about who's actually running a given well today.

sections.title: Faulkner County Circuit Clerk records and reconstructing family ownership
sections.html:
The Circuit Clerk's office in Conway holds the county's recorded deeds, oil and gas leases, probate filings, and division orders. Given how many Faulkner County mineral interests have passed through multiple generations, often without a formal partition, and how much surface land has changed hands as the county has grown, reconstructing an accurate ownership picture is frequently more involved here than in more rural, less-developed counties.

The acquisition desk does that reconstruction as part of the offer process, working from whatever an owner has, a deed, a division order, an old lease, or a probate reference, and cross-checking against the Circuit Clerk's index and current operator filings before quoting a number.

faqs.q: Is Faulkner County part of the productive core of the Fayetteville Shale?
faqs.a: Yes, it's one of the most heavily and successfully drilled counties in the entire play, with well density and results generally among the strongest anywhere in the Fayetteville Shale.

faqs.q: Your family's land near Conway or Greenbrier has been developed or sold since the mineral rights were established. Do you still own them?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it depends on how the mineral estate was handled in the subsequent sales or subdivision deeds. The acquisition desk checks your specific chain of title to confirm before making an offer.

faqs.q: Why does the operator name on your royalty statement keep changing?
faqs.a: Southwestern Energy's original Fayetteville Shale position moved to Flywheel Energy in 2018 and then to BKV Corporation in 2021. A name change on your statement over the years reflects one of those transactions.

faqs.q: How much has a typical Faulkner County well declined from its original production?
faqs.a: Substantially. Fayetteville Shale wells lose most of their output within the first few years and now sit on a long, low-volume decline tail, which is where most legacy Faulkner County wells are today. The acquisition desk prices based on current output, not historical peak.

faqs.q: Several relatives inherited a share of the same Faulkner County interest. Can you still buy it?
faqs.a: Yes. The acquisition desk can confirm each person's exact fractional share through Faulkner County Circuit Clerk records in Conway and purchase individual shares without requiring every heir to sell at the same time.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in White County, AR
items.meta: White County mineral owners around Searcy, Beebe, and Judsonia often hold small, heir-split Fayetteville Shale interests. The acquisition desk untangles the title and make a cash offer.

sections.html:
White County sits on the eastern flank of the Fayetteville Shale, and most of the mineral interests the acquisition desk sees here came down through a family rather than a landman's lease.

Ask ten White County mineral owners how they came to own their interest and most of them will point to a grandparent's farm outside Searcy, Beebe, Bald Knob, or Judsonia, land that was in the family long before anyone drilled a Fayetteville Shale well nearby. That's the pattern in this county more than the classic story of a single operator leasing up a block. White County was drilled, but as flank acreage to the core counties to the west, which means well density is lower and ownership tends to be older, smaller, and split across more heirs.

That combination, thinner production plus fractional heirship, is exactly what an acquisitions desk has to price carefully rather than off a generic county average. The acquisition desk starts with what the title actually shows, then price the interest against real production, not a rumor of what a neighbor got.

sections.title: White County's Position on the Fayetteville Play
sections.html:
The core of the Fayetteville Shale sat in Van Buren, Cleburne, Faulkner, and Conway counties, with White County catching development on its western edge as operators extended the play outward. That means fewer wells per section here than in the core, and a mix of vertical and horizontal completions rather than the dense horizontal pattern you'd find further west. Some sections in the county never saw a well at all.

Flank position isn't a reason to write off an interest. It just means each tract needs to be checked individually against Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission well records rather than assumed to be producing the way core-county acreage usually is.

sections.title: Split Estates and Heirship Are the Norm Here
sections.html:
Because so much of White County's mineral ownership traces back to original farm and homestead tracts, it's common for an interest to have passed through two or three generations without ever being formally divided in the courthouse. The surface may have sold off separately decades ago while the minerals stayed with the family, which is the split estate situation the acquisition desk runs into constantly here.

When the acquisition desk researches a tract, the White County Circuit Clerk's deed and probate records in Searcy tell the acquisition desk whether the mineral interest was reserved at a sale, and whether every current heir is actually reflected on file. Cleaning that up is often the biggest single step toward a closing, more than the geology itself.

sections.title: What a Buyer Actually Prices on Flank Acreage
sections.html:
For a producing tract, the acquisition desk looks at the specific well or wells your interest is pooled with, their current output, and how much runway is left on the decline curve. For acreage with no well nearby, pricing is more speculative and leans on activity trends in the county and whether the depth and formation make future drilling plausible.

Values move with gas prices and with how much drilling interest exists in the area at a given time, so any number the acquisition desk discusses is tied to current comparable trades, not a flat figure that ignores what's actually happening in White County right now.

sections.title: Timeline From First Call to Closing
sections.html:
A straightforward tract with a single owner and clean title can close in a matter of weeks. Most White County files aren't that simple, though, so the acquisition desk builds in time to confirm heirs, pull any missing probate paperwork, and reconcile the deed history before the acquisition desk finalizes a number.

The acquisition desk handles that research rather than asking you to chase courthouse records yourself, and the acquisition desk won't put a firm offer in front of you until the title work backs it up.

faqs.q: Your family's land near Searcy has never had a well on it. Is the mineral interest worth anything?
faqs.a: It can be, though pricing undeveloped White County acreage is more speculative than pricing a producing tract. The acquisition desk looks at nearby well activity, depth, and formation to gauge realistic drilling interest before putting a number on it.

faqs.q: How do you know if your mineral interest is a split estate?
faqs.a: If the surface of the land was sold at some point but your family kept the minerals, or vice versa, that's a split estate. It shows up in the deed history at the White County Circuit Clerk's office in Searcy, and it's extremely common on older farm tracts in this county.

faqs.q: Several cousins inherited a share of the same royalty. Can you buy just your portion?
faqs.a: Yes. The acquisition desk regularly buys individual fractional shares from one heir without requiring the whole family to agree to sell, though the acquisition desk does need clean documentation showing your specific percentage.

faqs.q: Why would flank-of-the-play acreage sell for less than core Fayetteville Shale acreage?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Conway County, AR
items.meta: Own oil, gas, or mineral rights in Conway County, Arkansas? The acquisition desk evaluates legacy Fayetteville Shale fringe interests countywide and make a cash offer, title research included.

sections.html:
Conway County sits on the southern and western margin of the Fayetteville Shale trend, with Morrilton as its courthouse town and generally lighter drilling history than the play's core counties to the north and east.

During the Fayetteville Shale's boom years between roughly 2005 and 2012, operators leased broadly across central Arkansas, and Conway County's acreage was part of that push even though the county was never among the play's most productive. That leasing wave left behind a mix of outcomes for mineral owners here: some tracts were actually drilled and produced meaningful volumes, particularly toward the county's northern and eastern sections closer to Faulkner County, while a larger share of the county's leasehold was signed and then never developed at all.

If you own minerals anywhere in Conway County, from Morrilton itself out to smaller communities like Center Ridge or Hattieville, the acquisition desk underwrites your interest by checking the actual production and permit history for your specific section rather than applying a blanket assumption about what Fayetteville Shale acreage is worth.

sections.title: A margin county in the Fayetteville Shale story
sections.html:
The play's thickest, most productive shale runs through Faulkner and Van Buren counties. Conway County sits along the southern and western edge of that trend, which generally meant lower well density and more variable per-well results than the core. That's the honest geological starting point for any Conway County valuation, and it's why the acquisition desk does not price interests here off headline numbers from better counties elsewhere in the play.

Results do vary meaningfully within the county itself. Sections closer to the Faulkner County line saw more development than areas further south and west, so the acquisition desk treats "Conway County" as a range of outcomes rather than a single answer, and the acquisition desk checks your specific legal description before quoting anything.

sections.title: Undeveloped leasehold from the boom years
sections.html:
A significant share of Conway County's original Fayetteville Shale leasing never resulted in a drilled well. Operators leased aggressively across the wider region to hold acreage and later concentrated their drilling budgets on the best rock, which in many cases wasn't here. If your family's tract falls into this category, you'd own unleased or undeveloped minerals rather than an active producing royalty.

That's still a real, sellable asset, just a different one than a producing interest, and its value is tied more to potential future activity and nearby drilling than to current cash flow. The acquisition desk prices it as what it actually is rather than implying royalty income that doesn't exist.

sections.title: Operator history and legacy well status
sections.html:
Where wells were drilled in Conway County, most trace back to Southwestern Energy's original Fayetteville Shale development under its SEECO subsidiary. That position was sold to Flywheel Energy in 2018 and later acquired by BKV Corporation in 2021, so an operator name change on an owner's royalty statement over the years typically reflects one of those transactions rather than a problem with the interest itself.

Given how long ago most Conway County wells were drilled, and how far most have declined from their original production rates, current royalty income for a producing interest here is generally modest. The acquisition desk prices based on that current, decline-adjusted output, not the well's historical peak.

sections.title: Conway County Circuit Clerk records and confirming a family's ownership
sections.html:
The courthouse in Morrilton holds the county's recorded deeds, leases, probate filings, and division orders. Because a meaningful number of Conway County mineral interests have been held quietly by the same family for two or three generations without much active management, and often without a formal partition when the interest passed to multiple heirs, reconstructing exact ownership shares is frequently the real first step before any sale can move forward.

The acquisition desk works from whatever documentation an owner has, a deed, an old lease, a division order, or in some cases just a family name and a general location, and confirm current status and ownership through the Circuit Clerk's index rather than requiring a complete paper trail upfront.

faqs.q: Is Conway County part of the productive core of the Fayetteville Shale?
faqs.a: No, it sits on the play's southern and western margin, with generally lower well density and more variable results than core counties like Faulkner and Van Buren.

faqs.q: Was a well ever actually drilled on your family's Conway County tract?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific section. A significant share of the county's boom-years leasehold was never drilled. The acquisition desk checks current and historical operator and permit records for your legal description to answer directly.

faqs.q: If your lease from the 2000s never resulted in a well, is your mineral interest worthless?
faqs.a: No, but it's a different asset than a producing royalty interest. Undeveloped minerals still carry value tied to potential future activity and nearby drilling, and the acquisition desk prices them honestly as that kind of interest.

faqs.q: Why does the operator name on your royalty statement keep changing?
faqs.a: Most Fayetteville Shale wells in this area were originally drilled by Southwestern Energy, with the position later sold to Flywheel Energy in 2018 and then acquired by BKV Corporation in 2021.

faqs.q: Several family members inherited a share of the same Conway County interest. How does a sale work?
faqs.a: The acquisition desk can confirm each person's fractional share through Conway County Circuit Clerk records in Morrilton and purchase individual shares without requiring the entire family to sell together.

sections.html:
Cleburne County sits on the fringe of the Fayetteville Shale play, with Heber Springs as its courthouse town and Greers Ferry Lake as its economic center of gravity.

Cleburne County never became one of the headline counties of the Fayetteville Shale boom the way Faulkner and Van Buren did, but leasing activity between roughly 2005 and 2010 still reached most of the county, and a real, if more modest, base of legacy production exists here today. What makes this county distinct for mineral owners is the mix: tourism-driven land use around Greers Ferry Lake sitting directly on top of shale-gas leasehold that most owners have never thought much about.

If you own an interest anywhere in Cleburne County, from Heber Springs itself out to the smaller communities like Concord, Drasco, Edgemont, Greers Ferry, or Higden, the acquisition desk evaluates it against actual county-wide production data and current operator activity rather than a blanket assumption about what Fayetteville Shale acreage is worth.

sections.title: Where Cleburne County sits in the Fayetteville Shale play
sections.html:
The Fayetteville Shale's most productive rock runs through Faulkner and Van Buren counties, with Cleburne County sitting toward the eastern and southeastern fringe of that trend. Well density here has always been lower, and the wells that were drilled generally produced at more modest initial rates than the play's core. That's not a knock on the county, it's just the honest geological starting point for any valuation conversation.

Operators leased broadly across the county during the boom years regardless of exactly how good the rock was going to turn out to be, which means a meaningful share of Cleburne County acreage carries an old lease with no well ever drilled on it. If that's your situation, the acquisition desk treats it as undeveloped mineral acreage, a real asset, but a different one than a producing royalty interest.

sections.title: Operator history and who's actually running legacy wells today
sections.html:
Southwestern Energy, through its SEECO subsidiary, was the dominant original developer across the Fayetteville Shale, including whatever wells were drilled in Cleburne County. Southwestern sold its Fayetteville Shale position to Flywheel Energy in 2018, and Flywheel's assets were acquired by BKV Corporation in 2021. If your royalty statements have changed the operator name over the years, or if you're not sure who currently operates a well tied to your interest, that history explains most of the confusion the acquisition desk sees from owners in this county.

The acquisition desk checks current operator and production filings directly with the state before making an offer, rather than relying on whatever name last appeared on a statement that may be years old.

sections.title: Greers Ferry Lake, resort development, and mineral severance
sections.html:
A meaningful share of Cleburne County's economy runs through tourism and lake-area real estate around Greers Ferry, including the Fairfield Bay community that spans into Van Buren County. Because so much of this land has changed hands for residential and recreational purposes, mineral rights here don't always track cleanly with surface ownership the way they do on land that's stayed in one family's hands. Some lake-area lots were sold with minerals reserved by a prior owner or developer; others carried the full mineral estate along with the surface.

Before assuming you own minerals under a lake-area property, or assuming you don't, it's worth checking the actual deed history. The acquisition desk does that as a standard part of evaluating any Cleburne County interest, since guessing in either direction can lead an owner to walk away from a real asset or waste time pursuing one that isn't there.

sections.title: Cleburne County Circuit Clerk records and confirming ownership
sections.html:
The Circuit Clerk's office in Heber Springs holds the county's recorded deeds, oil and gas leases, probate filings, and division orders. Because many Cleburne County mineral interests have passed through two or three generations without a formal partition, several family members frequently hold an undivided fractional share of the same tract without a clear written record of who owns exactly what percentage.

The acquisition desk uses the Circuit Clerk's index to reconstruct that chain of title as part of any offer, working from a deed, an old lease, a probate reference, or in some cases just a family name if that's all an owner has. You're welcome to verify the acquisition desk's research independently at the courthouse; the acquisition desk is not asking anyone to take the acquisition desk's word for it on something as important as their family's mineral ownership.

faqs.q: Is Cleburne County part of the productive core of the Fayetteville Shale, or more of a fringe area?

faqs.q: Why does the operator name on your royalty statement keep changing?
faqs.a: Most Fayetteville Shale positions in this area were originally developed by Southwestern Energy, sold to Flywheel Energy in 2018, and then acquired by BKV Corporation in 2021. A name change on your statement usually reflects one of those transactions, not a problem with your interest.

faqs.q: Your family owns a lake-area lot near Greers Ferry or Fairfield Bay. Do you have mineral rights?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific deed history for your lot. Some development-era sales reserved minerals for a prior owner; others conveyed the full estate. The acquisition desk checks your chain of title to confirm before assuming either way.

faqs.q: What if your lease from the Fayetteville Shale boom years never resulted in a drilled well?
faqs.a: You'd own unleased or undeveloped minerals rather than an active producing royalty. That's still a real asset, priced based on nearby activity and formation potential, and the acquisition desk is direct about the distinction when the acquisition desk makes an offer.

faqs.q: Several relatives inherited a share of the same interest together. Can you still buy it?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Van Buren County, AR
items.meta: Own minerals under Clinton, Shirley, or Fairfield Bay? The acquisition desk prices Van Buren County Fayetteville Shale tracts off current royalty checks, not guesswork. Get a cash offer.

sections.html:
Van Buren County was one of the four original core counties of the Fayetteville Shale, and most of the acreage here has been producing gas for well over a decade.

Southwestern Energy's SEECO subsidiary, along with XTO and later Chesapeake, drilled the Fayetteville Shale hard through Van Buren County starting around 2005, stacking horizontal wells into large pooled units around Clinton, Shirley, Choctaw, and Fairfield Bay. Two decades on, most of that gas is well past its steepest decline, and a lot of the working interest has changed hands two or three times since the boom, moving from the original operators into smaller consolidators. If you're a mineral owner here, your royalty check today is telling you something specific about where that well sits on its curve, and that number is the starting point for any conversation about selling.

The acquisition desk looks at Van Buren County the way an acquisitions desk looks at any mature shale play: trailing production, remaining reserves, operator identity, and how many other tracts are still held by production in the same unit. That's different from a flat per-acre number pulled off a map.

sections.title: The Fayetteville Shale Build-Out Here
sections.html:
Van Buren County sits inside the original four-county core of the Fayetteville Shale, alongside Cleburne, Faulkner, and Conway. SEECO drove most of the horizontal development, with pooled drilling units stretching for hundreds of acres around Clinton and Shirley in particular. Well density in the county core is high compared to the flank counties further east, which usually means your tract is captured in a unit with multiple producing wells rather than a single marginal one.

That density cuts both ways. It gave a lot of small tracts production they wouldn't have gotten drilled on their own, but it also means your royalty interest is often diluted across a large pooled unit, so a check that looks modest may still represent a fair share of a genuinely productive well.

sections.title: What the Clinton Courthouse Records Actually Show
sections.html:
The Van Buren County Circuit Clerk's office in Clinton holds the recorded lease, any Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission integration order that pooled your tract, and the probate file if the interest passed through an estate. Before the acquisition desk makes an offer the acquisition desk pulls that chain, because a division order percentage that hasn't been updated since a 2009 heir split is one of the most common reasons an owner's royalty check doesn't match what the acreage would suggest.

If your family's interest came down from a grandparent who never leased directly, and everything since has run through a pooling order, that's normal for this county. It just means the title work takes a little longer, not that the interest is worth less.

sections.title: Reading a Royalty Check This Far Into the Decline
sections.html:
Fayetteville Shale wells follow a steep first-year decline and then flatten into a long, low-volume tail, and most Van Buren County wells are firmly in that tail now. A check that's a fraction of what it was in year one isn't a sign the well is done; it's the normal shape of a shale gas curve at this age. The real question for pricing a sale is the current base decline rate and how many years of that tail are likely left at today's gas prices.

That's also why the acquisition desk prices off trailing production and comparable recent trades in the unit, not off a headline dollar-per-acre figure someone quotes from a different play. Two tracts in the same section can be worth different amounts depending on which wellbore they're pooled with.

sections.title: Deciding Between a Lump Sum and Holding the Royalty
sections.html:
Holding a small royalty interest through decades of decline means collecting shrinking checks, filing them on your taxes every year, and eventually dealing with the interest as part of an estate. Selling converts that long tail into one payment now, priced against what the remaining production is actually worth given current activity in the unit.

There's no single right answer. Owners who want liquidity now, who are settling an estate, or who'd rather not track a check that varies with gas prices tend to sell. Owners who believe the county could see renewed drilling, or who simply want the income stream, tend to hold. The acquisition desk will walk you through both sides before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Do you own minerals under your Van Buren County land even if you has never received a check?
faqs.a: Possibly. Many tracts in the county were pooled into a unit by an Arkansas Oil and Gas Commission integration order even if the owner never signed a lease directly. If your interest is small enough, or the division order was never updated with your address, checks can go unpaid or get held. The acquisition desk can research the AOGC docket and county records to find out what you actually hold.

faqs.q: Is your tract in the core of the Fayetteville Shale or on the edge of it?
faqs.a: Van Buren County is one of the four original core counties, so most sections here saw multiple horizontal wells rather than a single test well. Core position generally means more consistent production history, which is one of the factors that goes into pricing your interest.

faqs.q: How do heirs split a royalty when the original owner's division order is decades old?
faqs.a: The operator's division order department typically requires a probate file or affidavit of heirship before it will split payments among multiple descendants. This is one of the most common reasons Van Buren County royalty checks stall out, and it's something the acquisition desk helps sort out as part of closing a sale.

faqs.q: How is a producing tract priced differently than one that's never been drilled?
faqs.a: A producing tract is priced primarily off trailing royalty income and the well's remaining decline curve, verified against county and operator records. An undeveloped tract is priced more speculatively, based on activity nearby and whether the formation and depth make it a realistic drilling target.

faqs.q: How long does closing take once you accept an offer?
faqs.a: Once title is confirmed against the Circuit Clerk's records in Clinton, most Van Buren County closings move in a few weeks. Estates or unresolved heirship can add time, but the acquisition desk handles that title work rather than passing it back to you.

The Busey #1 discovery well blew in southwest of town in 1921 and turned a sleepy county seat into a boomtown almost overnight. A century later, Union County mineral owners are sitting on two overlapping stories: thousands of shallow, stripper-rate Smackover oil wells drilled decades ago, and a brand-new lithium brine industry racing to catch up to the bromine plants that have run here since the 1950s.

If you hold an interest that traces back to those early 1920s leases, or you inherited a fractional share nobody in the family has looked at closely, the acquisition desk underwrites Union County paper every week and can tell you fairly quickly whether what you own is worth carrying or worth selling.

sections.title: A century of Smackover production, and what it means for value today
sections.html: Most legacy oil and gas interests around El Dorado are attached to wells that peaked long ago and now produce at stripper rates, sometimes just a few barrels a day split across dozens of heirs. That doesn't make the interest worthless, but it does mean valuation has to be built off actual decline data and current operator activity in your specific section, not off what a 1980s lease once paid. The acquisition desk pulls the well history, check who currently operates it, and price against comparable Union County trades before the acquisition desk quotes anything.

sections.title: The lithium brine layer changes the math for some tracts

ExxonMobil's move into south Arkansas lithium in 2023, built on a large block of legacy Smackover leasehold around Union County, put brine rights on the map for owners who had never thought about them. Bromine extraction from the same formation has been running here for decades through the plants that operate east and south of town, so the infrastructure and the regulatory framework for produced brine already exist. Whether your deed's mineral language actually captures brine-hosted lithium, as opposed to just oil and gas, is a title question worth answering before you assume you're sitting on emerging-play acreage.

The acquisition desk treats brine potential as a real but separate variable from your oil and gas history. A tract can be a marginal legacy oil play and still carry brine upside, or the reverse, depending on formation depth and where you sit relative to the active leasehold blocks.

situations.title: Owner Situations

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: Received a mailer offer for your Smackover or Fayetteville mineral rights? The acquisition desk benchmarks it against actual production and lease data before you sign anything.

sections.html:
The letter in your mailbox with a number and a deadline is designed to get you to decide fast, and fast decisions on a permanent asset transfer usually favor the buyer.

If you own minerals in south or north-central Arkansas, particularly anywhere near current Smackover brine leasing activity or a producing Fayetteville well, you've probably gotten at least one unsolicited letter offering to buy your interest, often with a specific dollar figure and language suggesting the offer won't last. Some of these are legitimate offers from real buyers pricing off real data. Some are low, opportunistic numbers betting that you won't check them against anything before signing.

The acquisition desk is glad to benchmark any offer you've received, whether or not you ultimately sell to the acquisition desk. Send the acquisition desk the offer letter along with your county and legal description, and the acquisition desk will tell you honestly whether the number looks reasonable against what the acquisition desk can see in production and lease data, or whether it looks low.

sections.title: Why Mailer Offers Vary So Widely
sections.html:
Buyers sending unsolicited mailers range from well-capitalized acquisition companies with real production data behind their numbers to smaller operations working off nothing more than a county tax roll and a hunch. The letter itself rarely tells you which one you're dealing with, and the number can differ by a wide margin from what a data-backed offer would produce, in either direction, without the letter explaining why.

A mailer that arrived because your name showed up on a courthouse deed search, without the sender ever checking your interest's actual production or lease status, is a different kind of offer than one from a buyer who pulled your division order and priced against real numbers. The acquisition desk will tell you which situation your offer looks like once the acquisition desk sees it.

sections.title: What to Check Before Signing Anything
sections.html:
Ask whether the offer reflects your actual production history, if your interest is producing, or is it a flat, generic number that doesn't reference your specific well or lease at all. Check whether the deed you're being asked to sign matches what was described in the letter, since the actual transfer document is the only thing that legally matters, not the cover letter's language. And don't treat a stated deadline as real pressure; a fair offer on your mineral interest doesn't expire in a week, and any buyer implying it does is using urgency instead of a strong number to get you to sign.

If the letter references a specific well, lease, or division order number, that's a reasonable sign the buyer did real homework. If it's a form letter with your name inserted and no specifics about your actual interest, treat the number with more skepticism.

sections.title: How the acquisition desk benchmarks an Offer
sections.html: Send the acquisition desk a copy of the offer, your county, and your legal description or division order if you have one. The acquisition desk will pull whatever production or lease data is available for your specific tract and tell you where the mailer's number falls relative to what the acquisition desk would offer and what a reasonable range looks like given current activity. If the acquisition desk's number comes in higher, the acquisition desk will explain why. If the mailer's offer is already fair, the acquisition desk will tell you that too rather than manufacture a reason to compete.

sections.title: No Obligation Either Way
sections.html: Benchmarking an offer doesn't commit you to selling to anyone, including the acquisition desk. Some owners use this to confirm they should accept the mailer offer as-is, some decide to negotiate the original offer up once they have a comparable number in hand, and some decide to sell to the acquisition desk instead. All three are reasonable outcomes, and the acquisition desk is not going to pressure you toward the third one.

faqs.q: Is it worth getting a second opinion on a mailer offer?
faqs.a: Generally yes, especially for a permanent asset transfer. A quick benchmark against actual production or lease data costs you nothing and either confirms the offer is fair or shows you it isn't.

faqs.q: How do you know if the mailer offer used real data about your interest?
faqs.a: Check whether it references a specific well, lease, or division order tied to your tract, versus a generic form letter with just your name and county filled in. Specificity is a reasonable, though not perfect, signal of real homework.

faqs.q: Should you worry about the deadline in the letter?
faqs.a: Not typically. A fair offer on a mineral interest doesn't need to expire in a few days, and a stated deadline is more often a pressure tactic than a reflection of real time constraints on the buyer's side.

faqs.q: Will benchmarking your offer with you obligate you to sell to you?
faqs.a: No. The acquisition desk will give you an honest read on the offer whether or not you ultimately sell to the acquisition desk, or to anyone at all.

faqs.q: What if the mailer offer is actually higher than what you'd offer?
faqs.a: The acquisition desk will tell you that directly if it's true. The acquisition desk's goal is an honest benchmark, not a guaranteed higher number, and there's no advantage to the acquisition desk in pretending otherwise.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Inherited Smackover, Fayetteville, or Arkoma mineral rights in Arkansas? The acquisition desk helps heirs confirm ownership, price the interest, and decide keep vs. sell.

sections.html:
Most heirs who inherit Arkansas minerals didn't ask for the decision that comes with them, and the first honest step is figuring out what was actually inherited.

A mineral interest is one of the more unusual things to inherit, because unlike a house or an account balance, it doesn't come with a clean number attached. You might inherit a fraction of a producing Smackover royalty that's been paying steadily for decades, a stake in Fayetteville acreage that's never seen a well, or a piece of both split across several tracts your grandparent accumulated over a lifetime, and the paperwork alone rarely tells you which situation you're in.

The acquisition desk works with heirs constantly, at every stage from the estate not yet being probated to interests that were distributed years ago and are only now being reconsidered. The acquisition desk's first job is helping you figure out exactly what you hold, and then giving you a real number for it, whether you decide to keep it or sell.

sections.title: Confirming What You Actually Inherited
sections.html:
The starting point is always the deed or the probate record showing your interest, and if you don't have either, the acquisition desk can typically trace it through county records once the acquisition desk knows the deceased's name and the general property location. From there the acquisition desk checks whether the interest is producing, non-producing, or leased-but-undrilled, and whether it sits in the Smackover, Fayetteville, or Arkoma trend, since each of those has a different production profile and, in the Smackover's case, a possible brine-royalty dimension worth checking separately.

A surprising number of heirs discover their inherited interest is smaller, or larger, than they assumed, because prior generations divided ownership among several children without anyone consolidating the fractions. Getting the actual decimal interest right matters before any pricing conversation makes sense.

sections.title: Keep, Consolidate, or Sell
sections.html:
Keeping a producing interest means ongoing, if modest, royalty income and continued exposure to whatever happens with the well and commodity prices, plus the administrative reality of tracking 1099 income and responding to lease correspondence. Consolidating makes sense if you're one of several heirs and want to buy out siblings or cousins to hold a larger combined interest, though it requires their cooperation and capital. Selling converts the interest, whatever its size, to cash now, which is often the simplest outcome for heirs who live far from Arkansas, don't want to manage a small fractional royalty long-term, or would rather have the money today than a trickle over years.

None of these is automatically the right answer. The acquisition desk will give you a real number for the interest so the keep-versus-sell decision is based on something concrete rather than a guess.

sections.title: Multiple Heirs, Different Preferences
sections.html: It's common for siblings or cousins who inherited together to disagree, one wants to hold for the income, another wants to cash out now. That's manageable: each heir generally owns their own undivided fractional share and can sell it independently without the others' agreement, unless the interest hasn't yet been formally distributed out of the estate. The acquisition desk can buy one heir's portion while others keep theirs, which resolves the disagreement without forcing a family vote.

sections.title: If the Estate Hasn't Been Probated Yet
sections.html: If your loved one passed away and the mineral interest is still technically titled in their name, it needs to move through probate, or in some cases a simpler affidavit of heirship, before a clean sale can happen. The acquisition desk can point you toward what's typically needed and work on whatever timeline the probate process requires, but the legal work itself belongs with an estate attorney familiar with Arkansas probate procedure.

faqs.q: You inherited mineral rights but don't know exactly what you own. Where do you start?
faqs.a: Send the acquisition desk the deceased's name, the county, and whatever paperwork you have, even if incomplete. The acquisition desk can trace deed and probate records to confirm your exact interest before any pricing conversation.

faqs.q: Should you keep an inherited mineral interest or sell it?
faqs.a: It depends on whether it's producing, how you feel about ongoing administrative upkeep like 1099 tracking, and whether you'd rather have steady, modest income or a lump sum now. The acquisition desk will give you a real valuation so the decision is based on actual numbers.

faqs.q: Your siblings and you inherited together and disagree on selling. What are your options?
faqs.a: Generally each heir owns their own undivided share and can sell independently without the others' agreement, once the interest has been distributed. The acquisition desk can buy one heir's portion while the rest keep theirs.

faqs.q: The estate hasn't been through probate yet. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Title typically needs to pass out of the deceased's name first, through probate or an affidavit of heirship for simpler estates. The acquisition desk can work on whatever timeline that process takes and tell you what documentation the acquisition desk will need once it's underway.

faqs.q: Does it matter which formation the inherited interest is in?
faqs.a: Yes. Smackover, Fayetteville, and Arkoma interests each have different production and decline profiles, and Smackover tracts may carry an additional brine-royalty question worth checking separately. The acquisition desk evaluates each according to its own formation and production history.
